sets.title: Lakes of Bengaluru
sets.text: Bengaluru was once known as a city of a thousand lakes, built by farmers and local chieftains to catch the scant rain and recharge wells. These tanks were linked by channels, so that an overflow from one fed the next, and entire neighbourhoods drew their water from them. As the city grew into a technology hub, many lakes were filled to make way for apartments, bus depots and roads. Today fewer than a hundred survive, and several of those are choked with sewage. Citizen groups have begun to clean a few, removing silt, planting reeds at the edges and fencing off dumping spots. Engineers admit that restoring one lake achieves little unless the channels that connect it are also restored, and these are now buried under buildings. Still, a cleaned lake brings back egrets and kingfishers within a year, which encourages volunteers. The lesson, say the activists, is that a city that forgets how it once stored water will pay dearly when the monsoon fails.

sets.title: The Last Weavers of Pochampally
sets.text: In the lanes of Pochampally, the click of a handloom still begins before sunrise. The ikat technique practised here requires the yarn to be tied and dyed in patterns before it is woven, so that a design appears only when the cloth is on the loom. A single sari can take a family a week or more. Power looms in larger towns now copy these patterns in a day and sell them at half the price, and many young people in weaving families prefer jobs in hotels or call centres. Cooperative societies have responded by finding urban buyers, promoting a geographical indication tag that marks genuine work, and holding workshops for designers who wish to experiment with colour. Some weavers welcome these changes, while others fear that fashion will eventually reduce their craft to a passing trend. One elderly master says he does not mind who wears his cloth, so long as someone still wishes to learn how it is made.

sets.title: Why Trains Run Late in Winter
sets.text: Every December, northern India wakes to a blanket of fog, and railway timetables begin to fall apart. Drivers cannot see signals from a safe distance, so trains must crawl through the very stretches where they would normally move fastest. A delay of an hour on one route soon spreads across the network, because the same rakes and crews are needed for the next journey. The railways have fitted many locomotives with devices that warn a driver of an approaching signal even when it cannot be seen, and this has prevented accidents. Yet the devices only make travel safer; they do not make it faster, and passengers still wait for hours on cold platforms. Some commuters feel the railways should simply cancel trains in the worst weeks and give refunds, which would at least let people plan. Officials respond that cancelling services would strand those who have no alternative, and that a late train is still better than none.

sets.title: Cricket Without a Stadium
sets.text: In many Indian towns, the first cricket ground is not a ground at all but a lane, a terrace or a patch of dry field between houses. Children use a taped tennis ball, a plank for a bat and a wall for stumps, and they invent rules to suit the space: a hit into a neighbour's window is out, and a catch off the electric wire does not count. These rules vary from street to street, and arguments over them are a part of the game. Coaches who select players for academies sometimes say that such play teaches things no net session can, for it forces a young batter to improvise against bowlers of every kind. Others point out that talent born in a lane still needs proper coaching, a good diet and access to turf pitches. India's cricketing strength, in this view, comes from the match of an enormous number of casual players with a thin but improving system that finds the best of them.

sets.title: The Cost of a Free Ride
sets.text: Several state governments now offer free bus travel to women, and the early results are visible at every crowded stop. More women are travelling to markets, hospitals and workplaces, and some bus conductors report that female passengers now outnumber men at peak hours. Supporters say the policy returns a daily saving of a few hundred rupees to families, expands women's access to jobs and makes the city more welcoming. Critics counter that revenue falls, buses become overcrowded and the cost lands on the state treasury, which must pay the transport corporation to make up the difference. An economist who studied the scheme says that the policy may well pay for itself if it helps even a small share of women enter paid work, but that the evidence is yet to be gathered over several years. She adds that no scheme is free; the real question is who pays and what is received in return. Until the numbers are in, both camps have reason for caution.

sets.title: Silence in the Examination Hall
sets.text: For many Indian families, a school board examination is the most anxious event of the year. Parents lower the volume of the television, relatives postpone visits and neighbours ask quietly about the date of the Mathematics paper. Psychologists point out that this collective hush, though well meant, can increase pressure, since a child begins to feel that the whole household's happiness depends on a few marks. Some schools have therefore started to hold sessions in which parents are advised to treat examination months as a normal part of life: to keep regular meals and sleep, to allow short games and to avoid comparing children with cousins. Teachers report that students who study in such relaxed homes tend to score as well as, and often better than, those in tense ones. The change is slow, because a culture of anxiety is not undone by one workshop, but a growing number of families are beginning to realise that calm is not the same as silence.

sets.title: Salt Pans of Kutch
sets.text: Each year, as the monsoon retreats from the Little Rann of Kutch, thousands of families called agariyas walk onto the dry, cracked plain and begin to extract salt from underground brine. They pump the water into shallow pans, rake it as it crystallises and carry the harvest in baskets to the edge of the desert. The work continues through the scorching months, when the white surface reflects sunlight so fiercely that many workers suffer from damaged eyes and cracked feet. Though India is among the largest producers of salt in the world, the people who produce it are among its poorest, for the price they receive from traders is low and unsteady. Welfare groups have begun to supply sunglasses, rubber boots and solar-powered pumps in place of diesel engines, which reduces both costs and smoke. Some families, however, remain in debt to the traders who advance them money before the season starts. Until that cycle is broken, one volunteer observes, the salt will continue to taste sweeter to the buyer than to the maker.

sets.title: The Art of the Monsoon Trek
sets.text: Every July, groups of college students from Pune and Mumbai head into the Sahyadri hills to trek among forts built by Maratha rulers centuries ago. Streams run across the paths, mist hides the next ridge and the grass is slippery, yet the number of trekkers rises each year. Local villagers, who once saw few visitors, now earn from guiding, selling tea and renting rooms. This has also brought problems. Plastic wrappers litter the forts, and an overcrowded weekend can leave a narrow staircase dangerously packed. Forest officials say that some visitors enter restricted areas and light fires, and rescue teams are called out almost every weekend. A few trekking clubs have therefore begun to carry back all the waste they find and to insist that members register with the local authorities before setting out. They argue that a hill belongs both to those who love to climb it and to those who live beneath it, and that love without care soon destroys what it admires.

sets.title: The Auto-Rickshaw Driver's Day
sets.text: By five in the morning, Murugan has washed his auto-rickshaw outside his rented room in Chennai and laid a small garland on the dashboard. His first customers are usually fruit sellers heading to the market, and then come schoolchildren, office staff and, after sunset, tired families with bundles. The fare meter, he says, is a mixed blessing: it protects a passenger from being overcharged but also makes it easy for a rival to compare prices. Rising fuel costs and the arrival of app-based taxis have cut his earnings, but he has joined a driver's union that negotiates for fairer rates. His eldest daughter is studying engineering, and he hopes she will never need to sit behind a steering wheel for twelve hours a day. Yet he does not speak ill of his trade. Over twenty years, he has carried brides, patients and politicians, and every passenger, he says, leaves a small story behind on the seat.

sets.title: Libraries Without Walls
sets.text: In several districts of Kerala, a woman on a bicycle now carries a trunk of books from house to house, collecting the ones that have been read and leaving new ones in their place. The scheme, started by a panchayat to reach those who could not walk to the village library, has more than a thousand borrowers, many of them elderly women who had not held a book for years. Readers say they enjoy not only the stories but the weekly conversation with the person who brings them. Authorities admit the scheme's costs are small, for the librarians are volunteers and the books are donations, yet it has revived reading habits that television had pushed aside. Some critics point out that the collection is mostly in Malayalam and popular fiction, which limits its value for students. Organisers reply that the first aim is to bring people back to reading, and that other tastes will grow once the habit is rebuilt.

sets.title: Cooking Gas and the Kitchen
sets.text: For generations, women in rural India cooked over open fires of wood and dung, breathing smoke that doctors compare to the smoke of dozens of cigarettes a day. A national scheme that offered free connections for liquefied petroleum gas to poor households has brought a cleaner flame into more than eight crore kitchens. Health workers report fewer coughs among children, and women say they save hours that were once spent collecting firewood. Yet the numbers conceal a stubborn fact: many families take only one or two refills a year and go back to wood. The refill costs several hundred rupees, which can be a large sum when income is irregular. Researchers who visited such homes found that women often prefer the gas for quick tea but use wood for the large meals, which require much fuel. Unless the price of refills comes down, or a subsidy is made more regular, the cleaner kitchen may remain only partly achieved.

sets.title: Moving Between Two Languages
sets.text: A child growing up in Hyderabad may speak Telugu with grandparents, Urdu in the neighbourhood, Hindi in films and English at school, switching from one to another without noticing. Linguists regard this as a gift, since children who hear several languages tend to be quicker at shifting attention from one task to another. Some parents, however, worry that so many languages will confuse a child and cause delays in speech, and they therefore speak only English at home. Researchers say such fears are largely mistaken: a child may mix words in early years, but this fades, and the full vocabulary is usually larger than that of a child who knows one language. The real risk, they add, lies elsewhere, in the loss of the home tongue, which can fade when a family stops using it, taking with it songs, proverbs and the link with elders. A language, one researcher says, is not a burden to be carried but a house to be kept in repair.

sets.title: The Metro and the City
sets.text: When the metro first reached the old quarter of Kolkata, many shopkeepers feared that the digging would ruin their business. Instead, travel time between the northern and southern ends of the city fell from over an hour to about twenty minutes, and customers who had once avoided the crowded roads began to arrive in larger numbers. Commuters say they now choose homes by the distance to a station rather than to an office. Urban planners note that each new line also pushes up rents near stations, so that the poor who were meant to benefit most may be forced to move farther out. A few cities have tried to control this by reserving some housing near stations for lower-income families, though the results have been uneven. The metro, in this view, is neither a cure nor a curse. It is a powerful tool whose benefits depend on whom the city chooses to include when it draws the map of the new neighbourhoods.

sets.title: Cities and the Disappearing Sparrow
sets.text: A generation ago, the house sparrow was so common in Indian towns that it was hardly noticed. Today many city children have never seen one. Ornithologists link the decline to several changes: sealed concrete buildings with no gaps where birds could nest, shrinking gardens, fewer insects for chicks and the spread of mobile phone towers whose effect is still debated. Studies of the towers have produced inconsistent results, and some scientists caution against blaming a single cause. Citizen groups in cities such as Chennai and Delhi have begun to put up wooden nest boxes, leave out water and grain, and plant native shrubs. Early counts show a modest return of sparrows to some neighbourhoods. March 20 is observed as World Sparrow Day, and teachers use it to start discussions. A small bird, one volunteer says, is a good measure of a city's health, for when it leaves, other changes usually follow.

sets.title: Haggling in the Bazaar
sets.text: In an Indian bazaar, the first price quoted is rarely meant to be paid. A shopkeeper in Jaipur names a figure, the customer laughs and offers half, and a conversation begins which may involve tea, a family history and mutual praise of each other's cleverness. To a visitor accustomed to fixed prices, this can seem tiring, even unfair. Yet many traders see it as an exchange of respect: a buyer who bargains shows interest in the goods, while a seller who yields shows regard for the customer. Economists add that bargaining lets a shop charge different prices according to what each customer can afford, something a printed price tag cannot do. The practice is declining in malls and online stores, where convenience is prized above conversation. Some shopkeepers lament this, saying that without the bargaining the shop loses its character, and a customer, who is no longer a guest, becomes only a payment.

sets.title: Water Harvesting in Rajasthan
sets.text: In the arid villages of Alwar, a few earthen embankments called johads have changed the landscape. Built by villagers with local labour, each johad holds the monsoon rain behind a low wall and lets it seep slowly into the ground, so that wells upstream stay full long after the rains. Over twenty years, hundreds of such structures have helped revive a river that had dried up, and farmers who once left for cities during the dry season now grow a second crop. Engineers who first doubted the method now study it. What distinguishes the johad is not its technique, which is ancient, but the way it is managed: each village decides how the water is to be shared, and no outsider may impose a rule. Government programmes that have tried to copy the structures without that community control have mostly failed. Water, the villagers say, is easy to store but hard to share, and sharing is what the johad really teaches.

sets.title: The Gift of Boredom
sets.text: Children in Indian cities today have more activity than ever before: coaching on weekdays, music classes on weekends and an unending flow of videos on phones. Child psychologists have started to ask whether, in filling every hour, parents have removed something valuable: boredom. When a child has nothing to do, they explain, the mind begins to make its own entertainment, inventing a game, building a model from scrap or watching an ant for an hour. These are small acts, but they build patience and imagination, the very skills that scheduled activity does not teach. Some parents find this idea hard to accept, since empty time seems wasted time, and they fear that their child will fall behind. Experts do not suggest that all structured activity should be dropped; they recommend a small portion of the day left unplanned. They argue that the child who learns to sit with an empty afternoon will later be better able to sit with a difficult problem.

sets.title: A Wedding Season Economy
sets.text: Between November and February, a typical Indian wedding season sends a ripple through the economy that few other events can match. A single large wedding may employ caterers, florists, tent contractors, musicians, drivers, tailors and jewellers, many of them working on daily wages. Estimates of the sector run to several lakh crore rupees a year, and gold sales rise sharply in the weeks before the muhurat dates. Yet the same lavishness worries social critics, who point out that families often borrow heavily to match what neighbours spend, and carry the debt for years. Some communities have responded with collective weddings, where several couples marry in one ceremony at a modest cost. Others retain large celebrations but pare the guest lists. The hope, one economist suggests, is that a family will begin to measure a wedding by the happiness it brings and not by the number of dishes on the menu.

sets.title: Maps and Memory in Old Delhi
sets.text: The lanes of Old Delhi do not appear on a map in any useful way. They twist, double back and end in courtyards, and yet a rickshaw puller can reach any house without hesitation, because he navigates not by street names but by landmarks: the sweet shop at the corner, the mosque with a green dome, the doorway where a cow usually sleeps. Urban researchers who tried to digitise the area found that satellite maps missed hundreds of shops hidden in narrow passages. They then trained local boys to walk the lanes with phones and record each doorway, and the new map was soon more detailed than any official one. The project's leader says that this is a reminder that a map is a made thing, drawn by those who know the place, not a mirror of it. The boys, for their part, took pride in learning to see their own neighbourhood as a stranger would, and discovered how much they had always known.

sets.title: Trains of the Himalaya
sets.text: The narrow-gauge railway that climbs to Darjeeling from the plains was built in the 1880s to carry tea, and it still does so at a speed that a cyclist could match. Its small steam engines puff through the bazaars, passing so close to shops that a passenger could buy a cup of tea through the window. Modern roads have long been faster, and the railway earns less than it costs, yet it has been given heritage status and is kept running with the help of grants. Local people have mixed feelings about this. Some say the railway brings tourists whose spending supports guest houses and guides; others say the money spent on the toy train could be better used on roads and hospitals in the hills. A guard who has worked on the line for thirty years says he does not argue either way. He only notes that nobody has ever asked to stand on a highway just to watch it pass.

sets.title: Cash and the Kirana
sets.text: The neighbourhood kirana store has survived the arrival of supermarkets and online grocers in a way few experts predicted. Its advantages are simple: it is round the corner, it opens early and closes late, and the owner knows which family needs a small packet of tea until the end of the month. Many shops keep a ledger of credit, which functions as a rough form of lending to families that no bank would serve. Supply companies have noticed this and now offer shopkeepers phone applications to order stock, track sales and receive small loans. Some owners have embraced them; others worry that the large platforms will use the data to open competing outlets. A researcher who studied three hundred stores found that those that combined personal service with simple technology earned more than those that adopted neither. The kirana, she concludes, will not be defeated by the supermarket, but it may be changed by the supplier who decides to become a competitor.

sets.title: A Doctor in the Hills
sets.text: Dr Meena arrived in a mountain village in Uttarakhand twelve years ago with a medical degree and a plan to stay for two years. The nearest hospital was a day's walk, women in labour were carried on cots down steep paths and a simple infection could become fatal before help arrived. She trained local women as health workers to recognise danger signs, and installed a radio link with the district hospital. In the first five years, deaths during childbirth in the area fell sharply, and nearby villages began to send for her. Her colleagues in the city sometimes ask why she gave up a career where she could earn ten times as much. She does not reply with speeches. She says only that the question is a strange one, for a person who is useful in the place where she is needed does not feel that anything has been given up.

sets.title: The Language of Road Signs
sets.text: Anyone who has driven on an Indian highway has seen the signs that say 'Speed thrills but kills' and 'Better late than never'. Such slogans, painted with simple humour, are part of the national landscape, and safety officials say that a witty line is remembered longer than a stern warning. But the larger problem lies elsewhere. In many places, signs are missing, faded or hidden by hoardings, and a driver at night may not see a sharp curve until it is too late. A study of road accidents on a state highway found that more than half had occurred at points where a warning sign was absent or unreadable. Engineers therefore recommend reflective paint, standard symbols that do not depend on language and regular inspection of signs. Slogans may please a driver, they add, but only a clear sign will tell him when to slow down.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Bengaluru's lakes, once a connected water system, have largely been lost, and reviving them requires restoring the whole network.
Bengaluru has more lakes today than at any time in its history.
Technology companies are solely responsible for the loss of the city's lakes.
Egrets and kingfishers can survive only in cleaned lakes.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the decline of the lakes, notes local cleaning efforts and stresses that connecting channels matter. The other options are untrue or take a single detail as the whole.

questions.questionText: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The struggle of a traditional weaving craft to survive amid cheaper imitations and changing aspirations
The superiority of power looms over handlooms
The history of ikat in ancient India
The success of call centres in rural Telangana
questions.explanation: The passage describes ikat weaving, the threat from power looms and young people leaving, and the responses. The other options are either contradicted or not discussed.

questions.questionText: The main point the passage makes is that
options: winter fog disrupts train services, and safety devices reduce risk but do not restore punctuality
fog is the only cause of train delays in India
the railways have completely solved the problem of fog
commuters should avoid travelling by train in December
questions.explanation: The passage explains how fog causes cascading delays and that safety devices help with accidents, not speed. The remaining options are overstated or unsupported.

questions.questionText: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Informal street cricket nurtures talent that the formal system then has to identify and develop.
Street cricket should replace academy training.
Cricket rules are identical in every Indian town.
Tennis balls are better than leather balls for learning.
questions.explanation: The passage values lane cricket as a talent pool while noting the need for coaching and facilities.

questions.questionText: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: Free bus travel for women has clear benefits and clear costs, and its long-term worth is not yet established.
Free bus travel is certain to bankrupt the state.
Women should not be allowed to travel at peak hours.
Bus conductors are opposed to the scheme.
questions.explanation: The passage gives arguments of supporters and critics and an economist's caution that evidence is still awaited.

questions.questionText: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the pressure examinations create and the need for a calm, rather than a tense, household
the difficulty of the Mathematics paper
the benefits of postponing family visits
the abolition of board examinations
questions.explanation: The passage points to the pressure produced by a hushed home and advises normal routines instead.

questions.questionText: The passage is mainly concerned with (Passage: “Salt Pans of Kutch”)
options: the hard working conditions and economic insecurity of salt workers in Kutch
the history of salt trade across Asia
the benefits of diesel pumps in the desert
the superiority of Indian salt over imported salt
questions.explanation: The passage describes the labour of the agariyas, the health hazards and poor earnings, and some relief measures.

questions.questionText: The central idea of the passage is that
options: monsoon trekking brings livelihood and enjoyment to the Sahyadris but also demands responsible behaviour
the Maratha forts should be closed to visitors
villagers are opposed to tourism
trekking clubs are unnecessary
questions.explanation: The passage presents the growth in trekking, its benefits to locals and its harms, and ends by recommending care.

questions.questionText: What is the passage chiefly about?
options: The daily life, struggles and pride of an auto-rickshaw driver
The history of the fare meter in Tamil Nadu
The superiority of app-based taxis
Murugan's daughter's engineering course
questions.explanation: The passage follows his routine, difficulties and his attitude to his work.

questions.questionText: What is the main idea of the passage? (Passage: “Libraries Without Walls”)
options: A low-cost home book-delivery scheme in Kerala has revived reading among those who could not reach libraries.
Television has completely replaced reading in Kerala.
Students should read only popular fiction.
Panchayats should shut down their libraries.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the scheme, its readers, its low cost and a criticism with a response.

questions.questionText: The passage is mainly about (Passage: “Cooking Gas and the Kitchen”)
options: the benefits and limits of a clean cooking-fuel scheme for poor households
the dangers of tea drinking
a ban on firewood in villages
the cost of cigarettes in rural areas
questions.explanation: The passage notes the scheme's gains, then explains why many families still use wood.

questions.questionText: What is the central idea of the passage? (Passage: “Moving Between Two Languages”)
options: Growing up with several languages is beneficial, and the greater danger is losing the home language.
Children should learn only English.
Mixing words proves that a child is slow.
Hindi films harm language development.
questions.explanation: The passage dispels the fear of confusion and warns about loss of the home tongue.

questions.questionText: The passage is chiefly concerned with
options: the benefits of a metro system and the need to protect the interests of the poor near stations
the history of Kolkata's old quarter
the closure of shops caused by construction
the disadvantages of living close to offices
questions.explanation: The passage lists benefits (shorter travel) and a risk (higher rents), concluding that the outcome depends on inclusion.

questions.questionText: The main idea of the passage is that (Passage: “Cities and the Disappearing Sparrow”)
options: the house sparrow has declined in cities for multiple reasons, and citizen efforts are helping some recover
mobile phone towers are the only cause of sparrow decline
sparrows have disappeared completely from India
nest boxes are harmful to birds
questions.explanation: The passage lists several causes and local conservation efforts producing modest recovery.

questions.questionText: What is the main idea of the passage? (Passage: “Haggling in the Bazaar”)
options: Bargaining in Indian bazaars is a social and economic practice that is being displaced by fixed-price shopping.
Fixed-price shopping is unfair to the poor.
Tourists should avoid bazaars.
Malls are cheaper than bazaars.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the social meaning and economic role of haggling and its decline.

questions.questionText: The central idea of the passage is that (Passage: “Water Harvesting in Rajasthan”)
options: community-managed johads have restored water in Alwar, and their success rests on local control as well as technique
modern dams are always inferior to johads
the river in Alwar has never dried up
engineers have rejected the johad method
questions.explanation: The passage says success came from both the structure and village management.

questions.questionText: What is the central idea of the passage? (Passage: “The Gift of Boredom”)
options: Children benefit from some unstructured, unplanned time.
Children should stop attending coaching classes.
Videos are the best teachers.
Parents should never plan their children's day.
questions.explanation: The passage argues for leaving a small portion of the day free, not abolishing all structure.

questions.questionText: The passage is mainly about (Passage: “A Wedding Season Economy”)
options: the economic significance of Indian weddings and the concern about the pressure to spend excessively
the history of the muhurat
why gold prices fall in winter
the closure of catering businesses
questions.explanation: The passage describes the wedding economy and criticism of lavish spending.

questions.questionText: The passage chiefly illustrates that
options: local knowledge can capture details that formal maps miss
satellite maps are always accurate
Old Delhi's lanes are straight and wide
rickshaw pullers cannot read maps
questions.explanation: The researchers' team of local boys produced a better map than official ones.

questions.questionText: What is the central idea of the passage? (Passage: “Trains of the Himalaya”)
options: The Darjeeling railway survives as a heritage line despite being slow and unprofitable, and people differ on its worth.
The railway should be closed immediately.
Roads in Darjeeling are slower than the train.
The railway earns large profits from tea transport.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the line, its financial position and the mixed local views.

questions.questionText: The passage mainly argues that
options: the kirana store remains resilient because of personal service and credit, while facing new technological pressures
supermarkets have destroyed all small shops
kirana owners refuse to use any technology
ledgers are illegal
questions.explanation: The passage explains the kirana's strengths and the challenges from platforms.

questions.questionText: What is the main idea of the passage? (Passage: “A Doctor in the Hills”)
options: A doctor's dedicated service has improved health in a remote village.
Rural India has no need of doctors.
City hospitals are inferior to village clinics.
Radio links are the sole solution to maternal deaths.
questions.explanation: The passage describes how she remained and brought about improvement.

questions.questionText: The passage is mainly about (Passage: “The Language of Road Signs”)
options: the importance of clear, well-maintained road signs in addition to witty slogans
the poetry of highway slogans
the ban on road hoardings
the speed limits on state highways
questions.explanation: The passage moves from slogans to the larger problem of missing or unreadable signs.
